\section*{Question 6}

The function \(f\) is defined by the power series
\[
f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n} x^{2 n}}{(2 n+1)!}=1-\frac{x^{2}}{3!}+\frac{x^{4}}{5!}-\frac{x^{6}}{7!}+\cdots+\frac{(-1)^{n} x^{2 n}}{(2 n+1)!}+\cdots
\]
for all real numbers \(x\).
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Find \(f^{\prime}(0)\) and \(f^{\prime \prime}(0)\). Determine whether \(f\) has a local maximum, a local minimum, or neither at \(x=0\). Give a reason for your answer.
\item[(b)] Show that \(1-\frac{1}{3!}\) approximates \(f(1)\) with error less than \(\frac{1}{100}\).
\item[(c)] Show that \(y=f(x)\) is a solution to the differential equation \(x y^{\prime}+y=\cos x\).
\item[(a)] \(f^{\prime}(0)=\) coefficient of \(x\) term \(=0\)
\(f^{\prime \prime}(0)=2\left(\right.\) coefficient of \(x^{2}\) term \()=2\left(-\frac{1}{3!}\right)=-\frac{1}{3}\)
\(f\) has a local maximum at \(x=0\) because \(f^{\prime}(0)=0\) and \(f^{\prime \prime}(0)<0\).
\end{itemize}
\[
4:\left\{\begin{array}{l}
1: f^{\prime}(0) \\

1: \text { critical point answer } \\

\end{array}\right.
\]
\begin{itemize}
\item[(b)] \(f(1)=1-\frac{1}{3!}+\frac{1}{5!}-\frac{1}{7!}+\cdots+\frac{(-1)^{n}}{(2 n+1)!}+\cdots\)
This is an alternating series whose terms decrease in absolute value with limit 0. Thus, the error is less than the first omitted term, so \(\left|f(1)-\left(1-\frac{1}{3!}\right)\right| \leq \frac{1}{5!}=\frac{1}{120}<\frac{1}{100}\).
\end{itemize}

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y^{\prime}=-\frac{2 x}{3!}+\frac{4 x^{3}}{5!}-\frac{6 x^{5}}{7!}+\cdots+\frac{(-1)^{n} 2 n x^{2 n-1}}{(2 n+1)!}+\cdots \\
& x y^{\prime}=-\frac{2 x^{2}}{3!}+\frac{4 x^{4}}{5!}-\frac{6 x^{6}}{7!}+\cdots+\frac{(-1)^{n} 2 n x^{2 n}}{(2 n+1)!}+\cdots \\
& x y^{\prime}+y=1-\left(\frac{2}{3!}+\frac{1}{3!}\right) x^{2}+\left(\frac{4}{5!}+\frac{1}{5!}\right) x^{4}-\left(\frac{6}{7!}+\frac{1}{7!}\right) x^{6}+\cdots \\
& \quad+(-1)^{n}\left(\frac{2 n}{(2 n+1)!}+\frac{1}{(2 n+1)!}\right) x^{2 n}+\cdots \\
&= 1-\frac{1}{2!} x^{2}+\frac{1}{4!} x^{4}-\frac{1}{6!} x^{6}+\cdots+\frac{(-1)^{n}}{(2 n)!} x^{2 n}+\cdots \\
&= \cos x
\end{aligned}
